A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EYEMULATOR work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated historical results.

before.justification: v2 reports original fine-tuning experiments, session-mode comparisons, component ablations, attention measurements, and qualitative examples in Section 4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 reports original six-backbone experiments and revised session-mode, ablation, and attention analyses in Tables 2–5, alongside retained earlier results in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The gaze extraction, Bayesian priors, pseudo-path generation, weighted SFT, token-level DPO, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. However, Section 3 and Appendix C explicitly adapt training from v2's full-parameter fine-tuning to LoRA/QLoRA adapters, changing which parameters are updated.

E1.justification: Both versions use EyeTrans gaze data from 27 programmers and the same Java-centered CodeXGlue completion, Java-to-C# translation, and Java-to-English summarization tasks. Additional training-data regimes and category breakdowns concern retained coverage; no new dataset, language, population, or task is evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated no-gaze baselines for Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, SmolLM3-3B, and Granite-Code-2B alongside the original three backbone comparisons. Table 4 also introduces reported Random-control comparisons; v2 named Random Attention in Section 3 but provided no corresponding result rows.

E3.justification: v3 introduces 200-example and full-data regimes across six 1B–3B backbones, replacing uniform full fine-tuning with task-selected LoRA/QLoRA configurations. The new study reports containment-inclusive Exact Match for code tasks and METEOR for summarization, instead of v2's multi-metric evaluation. It also reports a DeepSeek tokenizer correction, qualitative run selection, and a current attention evaluation using 24 held-out examples per task.

E4.justification: Table 3 reruns session-mode comparisons and expands category-level analysis. Table 4 extends ablations to summarization and additional backbones, while separate frequency, monogram, and bi/trigram removals give way to No rare/flow and Random comparisons. Table 5 recomputes and expands attention diagnostics across all three tasks. The earlier attention heatmaps and two appendix case studies are retained.

E5.justification: v3 newly identifies robustness seeds 42 and 12345 and adds p-values for the twelve attention comparisons in Table 5. The statistical test is unspecified, and main results remain selected point estimates without cross-seed dispersion or confidence intervals. The new seed disclosure does not establish an increase over a known v2 run count.

E6.justification: All 60 task scores from v2 Table 2 survive unchanged in v3 Table 6. New Table 2 adds 36 matched baseline–EYEMULATOR comparisons under revised conditions, including StarCoderBase full-data completion at 74.13 versus 99.62 Exact. Tables 3–5 replace or expand further results: v2's summarization entropy comparison of 88.2 versus 60.4 is replaced by a current-adapter diagnostic of 7.11796 versus 7.11802. These are different-setting results, not direct v2-to-v3 performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix A introduces a different formal Exact criterion: full credit for equality or substring containment in either direction. The earlier weighted H-Exact definition remains as an auxiliary metric. The mathematical construction of the proposed method is unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion replace headline CodeBLEU/BERTScore gains and direct attribution to replicated human attention with positive selected results across 36 model-task-regime cells. Claims now distinguish stronger code-task effects from smaller, recipe-sensitive summarization gains and describe complementary signals rather than confirmed causation. The conclusion also drops the under-1MB overhead claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets large attention shifts as evidence of substantially sharper human-aligned focus. v3 Sections 4.5 and 5 instead characterize attention changes as small, task-dependent diagnostics supporting the downstream results. The rewritten discussion explains task differences through preservation of code structure, tokenizer behavior, and recipe sensitivity, and develops the interpretation of complementary semantic and transition signals.

D1.justification: Section 3 and Appendix C replace the fixed FP32, 2e-5, single-L40S configuration with adapter ranks, gaze weight 4, task-dependent learning rates, bf16/4-bit precision, and L40S-class hardware. Validation/test counts are newly specified. Conversely, v2 Appendix A.2's attention-metric definitions disappear, and exact summarization recipes and tokenizer-correction instructions remain unspecified. Artifact access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive positioning relative to gaze-aware architectures, retrieval, code models, and preference learning remain the same. Bibliographic metadata, URL wrapping, and introductory related-work wording change without altering research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, evaluation summary, experimental setup, most result interpretations, discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v3 adds an explicit contribution list and acknowledgments, introduces a historical-results appendix, and moves and revises future work into Appendix E. The approach and most related-work prose remain stable.

P2.justification: The main results table is redesigned around six backbones and two data regimes, while the earlier table moves to Appendix B as Table 6. Session-mode and ablation tables are substantially restructured, attention diagnostics become a separate table, and a new gain heatmap appears as Figure 6. Existing plots and qualitative cases are retained with caption, placement, and numbering changes.

improvement.justification: v3 broadens empirical testing, supplies additional controls, and moderates v2's strong attention-causality interpretation. However, its all-positive headline depends on selected 'quality-safe' runs without explicit selection rules or seed-wise uncertainty, while the new code metric awards full credit for bidirectional containment. Removing attention-metric definitions also reduces reproducibility. These substantive benefits and evaluation/reporting drawbacks prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
